chem_ocra.8.1.summary: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions involves breaking down ionic compounds dissolved in water using direct electrical current. Unlike molten compounds, aqueous solutions contain competing ions from water (H+ and OH-), which determine the specific products formed at the inert electrodes. Mastering the rules for selective discharge at the anode and cathode, along with Practical Activity Group C2 (PAG C2), is essential for top-grade success.

core.p: When an ionic compound is dissolved in water to form an aqueous solution, water molecules partially dissociate into hydrogen ions (H+) and hydroxide ions (OH-). This means that during the electrolysis of an aqueous solution, there are competing ions present for each electrode. Understanding which ion gets discharged requires specific rules based on the reactivity series and the relative concentrations of the ions.
bullets: Water provides extra H+ and OH- ions alongside the ions from the dissolved ionic solute.
Inert electrodes (such as platinum or graphite/carbon) do not react with the electrolyte or the products.
Direct current (DC) must be used to ensure a one-way flow of electrons and prevent ionic reversal.

callouts.p: The breakdown of an ionic compound dissolved in water by the passage of electricity.
Pure water contains a very small concentration of H+ and OH- ions: H2O <--> H+ + OH-.

core.h: Cathode Competing Ions and Reduction Rules
core.p: At the negatively charged cathode, positively charged cations are attracted and undergo reduction by gaining electrons. However, because H+ ions from water are always present, there is always competition between the metal cation and the hydrogen ion.
bullets: Rule 1: If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen (e.g., sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium, zinc, iron), hydrogen gas is produced at the cathode.
Rule 2: If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen (e.g., copper, silver, gold), the pure metal is deposited at the cathode.
Reasoning: More reactive metals prefer to stay as positive ions in solution because they form very stable ionic bonds, whereas less reactive metals are easily reduced.

callouts.p: Students often assume the metal in the salt always plates out. Always check the reactivity series relative to hydrogen.
For hydrogen: 2H+ + 2e- -> H2. For copper: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu.

core.h: Anode Competing Ions and Oxidation Rules
core.p: At the positively charged anode, negatively charged anions are attracted and undergo oxidation by losing electrons. The competition here is between halide ions (chloride, bromide, iodide) and hydroxide ions (OH-).
bullets: Rule 1: If a concentrated halide solution (chloride, bromide, or iodide) is electrolysed, the respective halogen (chlorine, bromine, or iodine) is produced.
Rule 2: If the solution contains sulfate, nitrate, or is very dilute, oxygen gas and water are produced from the discharge of hydroxide ions.
Oxidation half-equation for hydroxide: 4OH- -> O2 + 2H2O + 4e- or 2OH- - 2e- -> O + H2O.

callouts.p: Halides (Cl-, Br-, I-) are discharged in preference to hydroxide ions unless the solution is extremely dilute.
AN OX: Oxidation occurs at the Anode (loss of electrons).

core.p: Electrolysing aqueous copper(II) sulfate using inert carbon electrodes demonstrates both sets of competing rules clearly. It is a classic OCR exam setup.
bullets: Ions present in solution: Cu2+, H+, SO42-, OH-.
At the cathode: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper metal is deposited as a brown solid (Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu).
At the anode: Sulfate is a complex ion and hydroxide is present, so hydroxide ions are discharged, producing oxygen gas and water (4OH- -> O2 + 2H2O + 4e-).
Visual observation: The blue colour of the copper sulfate solution fades as Cu2+ ions are removed.

callouts.p: Fading blue color confirms Cu2+ ions are being used up during electrolysis.

core.p: The electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine) is an important industrial process that produces three useful commercial products: chlorine, hydrogen, and sodium hydroxide.
bullets: Ions present: Na+, H+, Cl-, OH-.
At the cathode: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen gas is discharged (2H+ + 2e- -> H2).
At the anode: Chloride ions are present in high concentration, so chlorine gas is discharged (2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-).
Remaining solution: Na+ and OH- ions are left behind, forming an alkaline solution of sodium hydroxide (NaOH).

callouts.p: A concentrated aqueous solution of sodium chloride.
Never state that sodium metal is produced; it reacts instantly with water anyway.

core.p: Dilute sulfuric acid is effectively the electrolysis of acidified water. Because sulfuric acid provides extra H+ ions and sulfate ions, water is decomposed into its elements.
bullets: Ions present: H+, SO42-, OH-.
At the cathode: Only H+ ions are present, so hydrogen gas is produced.
At the anode: OH- ions are discharged in preference to sulfate, producing oxygen gas.
Overall volume ratio: Hydrogen gas produced is twice the volume of oxygen gas produced (V(H2) = 2 V(O2)), matching the formula of water (H2O).

callouts.p: Hydrogen to oxygen volume ratio is always 2:1 during water electrolysis.

core.h: Required Practical C2: Investigating Aqueous Electrolysis
core.p: PAG C2 requires students to investigate the products formed when different aqueous solutions are electrolysed using inert electrodes (carbon/graphite).
bullets: Apparatus: Beaker, DC power supply, carbon rod electrodes, crocodile leads, test tubes for gas collection.
Safety: Wear eye protection; perform chlorine or hydrogen gas collection in a fume cupboard or well-ventilated area.
Testing gases: Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white; oxygen relights a glowing splint.
Observing electrodes: Look for gas effervescence or metal plating.

callouts.p: An electrode that conducts electricity but does not chemically take part in the reaction (e.g., graphite).
Be ready to describe gas tests and safety precautions step-by-step.

core.p: Writing ionic half-equations for aqueous systems requires balancing atoms and charges using electrons (e-). Examiners award marks for correct species and balance.
bullets: Reduction at cathode (H+): 2H+ + 2e- -> H2
Reduction at cathode (Metal): Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu
Oxidation at anode (Halide): 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-
Oxidation at anode (Hydroxide): 4OH- -> O2 + 2H2O + 4e-

callouts.p: Electrons must be on the left for reduction (gaining) and on the right for oxidation (losing).

core.h: Effect of Concentration on Anode Products
core.p: The concentration of ions in solution can override standard discharge rules, particularly at the anode.
bullets: In a very dilute sodium chloride solution, oxygen is produced at the anode because water molecules/hydroxide ions predominate.
In a concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine), chlorine gas is produced at the anode because the high concentration of chloride ions forces their oxidation over hydroxide ions.
Concentration acts as a deciding factor when competing ions have close oxidation potentials.

callouts.p: High concentration of a halide ion overrides hydroxide discharge at the anode.

core.p: A quick reference table of OCR specification electrolytes, their competing ions, and resulting electrode products.
bullets: Memorise these exact pairs as they form the basis of standard exam application questions.

head: Electrolyte
Cathode Product
Anode Product
Reasoning
rows: Cu less reactive than H; OH discharged over SO4
Na more reactive than H; high Cl- concentration
Only H+ at cathode; OH- discharged over SO42-

callouts.p: Notice sulfate and nitrate ions are never discharged at the anode in GCSE aqueous electrolysis.

analogy.p: Imagine a nightclub door where different types of guests (ions) arrive. At the cathode club door, VIP metal guests who are less reactive (like copper) get in immediately, but standard guests (like sodium) are turned away, forcing hydrogen bouncers to take their place. At the anode club, if there is a massive VIP crowd of halide troublemakers, they get priority entry over the regular hydroxide crowd.

A solid electrical conductor used to make contact with an electrolytic solution.
An electrode that conducts electricity without participating in the chemical reaction.
The negative electrode where reduction and gain of electrons occur.
The positive electrode where oxidation and loss of electrons occur.
An equation showing how electrons are gained or lost by ions at an electrode.
The gain of electrons or decrease in oxidation state.
The loss of electrons or increase in oxidation state.
A concentrated aqueous solution of sodium chloride.
The process where ions lose their charge by gaining or losing electrons at an electrode.
A list of metals arranged in order of their decreasing chemical reactivity.

mistakes.w: Sodium metal is formed at the cathode during brine electrolysis
mistakes.r: Hydrogen gas is formed because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen

mistakes.w: Sulfate ions turn into sulfur dioxide at the anode
mistakes.r: Sulfate is a stable spectator ion; oxygen gas is produced from hydroxide ions

mistakes.w: Electrons flow through the aqueous solution
mistakes.r: Electrons flow through the external wires; ions move through the solution

mistakes.w: Carbon electrodes dissolve and disappear quickly
mistakes.r: Carbon/graphite is inert; though anodes can slowly react with oxygen to form CO2, they are classed as inert

mistakes.w: Copper sulfate solution stays dark blue throughout electrolysis
mistakes.r: The blue colour fades as copper ions are discharged and removed from solution

mistakes.w: Chlorine is produced at the anode of a dilute sodium chloride solution
mistakes.r: Oxygen is produced because chloride concentration is too low to override water discharge

exam.q: State what is produced at the cathode when aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using carbon electrodes.
model: Copper / copper metal / brown solid
exam.tip: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen.

exam.q: Explain why hydrogen gas, rather than sodium metal, is produced at the cathode during the electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride.
model: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
Hydrogen ions are discharged in preference to sodium ions

exam.q: Write the ionic half-equation for the formation of chlorine gas at the anode.
model: Allow proper balancing and state symbols if required
exam.tip: Check that electrons are on the right-hand side for oxidation.

exam.q: Describe the test for chlorine gas produced at the anode.
model: Damp litmus paper
Bleaches white

exam.q: Explain why the blue colour of copper(II) sulfate solution fades during electrolysis.
model: Cu2+ ions cause the blue colour
Cu2+ ions are discharged/removed at the cathode to form copper metal
exam.tip: Link the colour to the specific ion.

exam.q: Give two industrial uses of the products formed during the electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution.
model: Chlorine: making bleach / sterilising water / making plastics (PVC)
Sodium hydroxide: making soap / neutralising acids / making bleach
Hydrogen: making margarine / producing ammonia
exam.tip: Learn at least one direct use for each of the three brine products.

exam.q: Name the gas produced at the anode when dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed.
model: Oxygen / O2
exam.tip: Sulfate is not discharged; hydroxide from water forms oxygen.

exam.q: Describe how you would safely carry out PAG C2 to investigate the electrolysis of copper(II) chloride solution.
model: Set up beaker with copper chloride solution and carbon electrodes connected to DC power supply
Observe pink/brown solid deposited at cathode and pungent green/yellow gas (chlorine) at anode
Test gas with damp blue litmus paper showing bleaching
Wear eye protection and use fume cupboard due to chlorine toxicity
exam.tip: Include setup, observations, gas test, and safety.

worked.q: A student electrolyses copper(II) sulfate solution using carbon electrodes for 15 minutes. Describe all observations at both electrodes and write the half-equation for the anode reaction.
steps: Step 1: Identify ions present: Cu2+, H+, SO42-, OH-.
Step 2: Determine cathode product: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so pink-brown copper metal plates onto the cathode.
Step 3: Determine anode product: Hydroxide ions are discharged in preference to sulfate, producing bubbles of oxygen gas.
worked.ans: Cathode: Pink-brown solid deposited. Anode: Effervescence / bubbles of gas (oxygen). Half-equation: 4OH- -> O2 + 2H2O + 4e-.

worked.q: Explain the differences in anode products when electrolysing dilute sodium chloride versus concentrated sodium chloride (brine).
steps: Step 1: State ions present in both: Na+, H+, Cl-, OH-.
Step 2: Explain dilute case: Chloride ion concentration is low, so hydroxide ions are discharged, producing oxygen gas.
Step 3: Explain concentrated case: High concentration of chloride ions overrides water discharge, forcing chloride ions to lose electrons and form chlorine gas.
worked.ans: Dilute NaCl produces oxygen gas at the anode because hydroxide ions are discharged. Concentrated NaCl produces chlorine gas because the high concentration of chloride ions forces their oxidation.

chem_ocra.8.2.summary: These revision notes provide a comprehensive, Grade 9 analysis of electrolysis using inert and non-inert electrodes according to OCR C3.4e. They cover the fundamental differences between platinum or graphite inert electrodes and reactive copper or silver non-inert electrodes. Detailed sections explain electroplating, copper refining, half-equations, and practical applications, ensuring absolute mastery of the OCR Chemistry specification.

core.h: 1. Introduction to Inert versus Non-Inert Electrodes
core.p: Electrolysis relies on electrodes to transfer electrons into and out of the electrolyte. The choice of electrode material completely changes the chemical outcome of the process.
bullets: **Inert electrodes** do not participate in the chemical reactions during electrolysis.
Common inert electrode materials include **graphite** (carbon) and **platinum**.
**Non-inert electrodes** (reactive electrodes) actively take part by losing or gaining mass.
Copper and silver are typical non-inert electrodes used in industrial and laboratory processes.

callouts.p: An electrode that conducts electricity into the electrolyte but does not chemically take part in the reaction.
Graphite is cheap, has a high melting point, and contains delocalized electrons to conduct electricity.

fig.cap: Comparison setup showing an inert graphite electrode versus a reactive copper non-inert electrode in copper sulfate solution.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><rect x="60" y="80" width="100" height="120" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1e3a8a" stroke-width="2" rx="5"/><rect x="240" y="80" width="100" height="120" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1e3a8a" stroke-width="2" rx="5"/><rect x="90" y="50" width="15" height="80" fill="#475569" stroke="#0f172a"/><rect x="270" y="50" width="15" height="80" fill="#b45309" stroke="#78350f"/><text x="75" y="40" font-size="12" fill="#0f172a">Graphite (Inert)</text><text x="245" y="40" font-size="12" fill="#0f172a">Copper (Non-inert)</text><path d="M100 120 L300 120" stroke="#334155" stroke-dasharray="4"/></svg>

core.p: When inert electrodes are used, the electrode material remains unchanged throughout the process. Only ions from the ionic compound or water are oxidized and reduced.
bullets: During molten binary electrolysis, metal ions form at the cathode and non-metal atoms form at the anode.
During aqueous electrolysis, **H+** and **OH-** ions from water compete with the solute ions.
At the inert anode, halide ions discharge in preference to hydroxide, otherwise oxygen gas is produced.
At the inert cathode, less reactive metals (like copper or silver) discharge in preference to hydrogen.

callouts.p: Graphite anodes still slowly wear away over time because oxygen produced at high temperatures reacts with the carbon to form carbon dioxide.

core.p: When non-inert electrodes are made of reactive metals like copper, the electrode itself undergoes chemical change, usually dissolving or being coated.
bullets: The **anode** (positive electrode) loses mass as copper atoms lose electrons to form copper ions.
The **cathode** (negative electrode) gains mass as copper ions from the solution gain electrons to form solid copper atoms.
The concentration of copper ions in the electrolyte solution remains constant overall.
Oxidation always occurs at the anode; reduction always occurs at the cathode regardless of electrode type.

callouts.p: In copper purification, for every copper atom oxidized at the anode, one copper ion is reduced at the cathode.

core.p: Impure copper extracted from ore is purified industrially using electrolysis with non-inert electrodes on a massive commercial scale.
bullets: The **anode** is made of impure copper containing impurities like gold, silver, and platinum.
The **cathode** is made of pure copper which grows thicker as pure copper plates onto it.
The electrolyte is an aqueous solution of **copper(II) sulfate**.
Copper ions leave the impure anode, travel through the solution, and deposit onto the pure cathode.

callouts.p: Unreactive precious metal impurities that drop below the impure anode during copper refining to form a valuable sludge.

fig.cap: Industrial copper refining setup showing impure copper anode and pure copper cathode in copper sulfate solution.

core.p: Half-equations explicitly show the electron transfer occurring at each non-inert electrode during copper purification.
bullets: At the impure copper **anode** (oxidation): Cu (s) -> Cu2+ (aq) + 2e-
At the pure copper **cathode** (reduction): Cu2+ (aq) + 2e- -> Cu (s)
The rate of oxidation at the anode equals the rate of reduction at the cathode.
Impurities less reactive than copper fall to the bottom as anode sludge.

callouts.p: Always ensure charges and atoms balance. Electrons (e-) must be on the right for oxidation (loss) and on the left for reduction (gain).

core.p: Electroplating is a process that uses electrolysis to coat a thin layer of a metal onto an object, usually for appearance or corrosion protection.
bullets: The object to be plated is always made the **cathode** (negative electrode).
The plating metal is used as the **anode** (positive electrode) to replenish ions in solution.
The electrolyte must be an aqueous solution containing ions of the plating metal.
Common examples include silver-plating cutlery and nickel-plating car bumpers.

callouts.p: Object to be coated = Cathode. Metal used for coating = Anode.

core.p: To silver-plate a brass spoon, specific conditions and materials must be arranged in the electrolytic cell.
bullets: The brass spoon is connected to the **negative terminal** (cathode).
A pure silver bar is connected to the **positive terminal** (anode).
The electrolyte is silver nitrate solution, **AgNO3 (aq)**.
Silver atoms on the anode lose electrons, enter solution as Ag+, and plate onto the spoon.

callouts.p: Objects must be thoroughly cleaned with acid and abrasive paper before electroplating to remove grease and oxide layers for good adhesion.

core.p: At each electrode during electroplating, half-equations describe the exact movement of electrons.
bullets: At the silver **anode**: Ag (s) -> Ag+ (aq) + e-
At the object **cathode**: Ag+ (aq) + e- -> Ag (s)
The concentration of silver ions in the electrolyte remains constant throughout.
The coating thickness depends on current strength and duration of electrolysis.

callouts.p: The process of coating a metal object with a thin layer of another metal using electrolysis.

core.p: A clear structural comparison highlights how electrode reactivity alters the chemical dynamics of an electrolysis experiment.
bullets: Inert electrodes transfer current without changing mass (except slight graphite oxidation).
Non-inert electrodes actively dissolve (anode) or gain mass (cathode).
Inert cells typically produce gases like oxygen or chlorine at the anode.
Non-inert copper or silver cells transfer metal directly from anode to cathode.

head: Feature
Inert Electrodes
Non-Inert Electrodes
rows: Does not dissolve; gases often form

core.p: Students investigate electrolysis using inert and copper electrodes to observe products and mass changes.
bullets: Measure the initial mass of copper strip electrodes using a analytical balance.
Connect electrodes to a DC power pack in copper(II) sulfate solution for 20 minutes.
Remove, rinse with propanone or distilled water, dry, and re-weigh.
The anode loses mass while the cathode gains an equal mass of pure copper.

callouts.p: Failure to dry electrodes completely before re-weighing leads to inaccurate mass measurements due to trapped water.

analogy.p: Think of an electrolysis cell with non-inert electrodes like a market stall. The anode is a merchant who donates his own goods (metal atoms losing electrons to become ions), which are carried across the market square (electrolyte solution) and handed to a customer at the cathode (ions gaining electrons to become solid metal atoms). Where it breaks down: in a real market, money changes hands, but in electrolysis, only electrons flow through the external wires while ions move through the solution.

terms.d: An electrode that conducts electricity but does not take part in the chemical reaction.
An electrode that actively participates in the electrolytic reaction by losing or gaining mass.
Using electrolysis to coat a metal object with a thin layer of another metal.
The positive electrode where oxidation occurs.
The negative electrode where reduction occurs.
Unreactive impurities that fall below the anode during copper refining.
Loss of electrons.
Gain of electrons.
An ionic compound in molten or aqueous state that conducts electricity.
The industrial purification of impure copper using electrolysis.
An equation showing oxidation or reduction with electron transfer.
Direct current power source required to maintain constant electron flow direction.

mistakes.w: Saying oxidation happens at the cathode.
mistakes.r: Oxidation always occurs at the anode (oxidation is loss at anode - OLA).

mistakes.w: Stating that inert electrodes dissolve during copper refining.
mistakes.r: Inert electrodes do not dissolve; only non-inert copper anodes dissolve.

mistakes.w: Placing the object to be electroplated at the anode.
mistakes.r: The object to be plated must always be the cathode.

mistakes.w: Writing copper ion formula as Cu+.
mistakes.r: Copper ions in standard OCR chemistry spec points are Cu2+.
Half-equations must explicitly show electrons as e-.

mistakes.w: Stating electrolyte concentration changes in copper refining with copper electrodes.
mistakes.r: Electrolyte concentration remains constant because copper entering from the anode equals copper depositing at the cathode.

mistakes.w: Referring to graphite as a metal.
mistakes.r: Graphite is a non-metal form of carbon that conducts electricity.

exam.q: State what is meant by a non-inert electrode.
model: An electrode that takes part in the chemical reaction / dissolves or gains mass.
exam.tip: Learn standard definitions word for word.

exam.q: Explain why the copper anode loses mass during the purification of copper.
model: Copper atoms lose electrons
to form copper ions which enter the solution.
exam.tip: Always mention electron loss for anode oxidation.

exam.q: Write a half-equation for the reaction occurring at the cathode during copper electroplating.
model: -> Cu
exam.tip: Include state symbols if requested, but check balance first.

exam.q: Describe how an iron spoon can be silver-plated using electrolysis.
model: Iron spoon is connected as the cathode
Pure silver bar is connected as the anode
Electrolyte is silver nitrate solution
Silver ions gain electrons at the spoon to form a silver coating
exam.tip: Mention all three components: cathode object, anode metal, and electrolyte.

exam.q: Explain why the concentration of copper ions in the electrolyte remains constant when purifying copper using copper electrodes.
model: Copper atoms form ions at the anode at the same rate
as copper ions gain electrons to form copper atoms at the cathode.
exam.tip: Compare rates at anode and cathode.

exam.q: State two differences between inert and non-inert electrodes during electrolysis.
model: Inert electrodes do not take part in reactions, whereas non-inert electrodes do.
Inert electrodes do not change mass, whereas non-inert electrodes lose or gain mass.
exam.tip: Contrast mass and chemical participation clearly.

exam.q: Write the half-equation for the reaction at the impure copper anode.
model: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-
exam.tip: Oxidation half-equations have electrons on the right.

exam.q: Give one reason why graphite is often used as an inert electrode.
model: It conducts electricity / has a high melting point / is unreactive.
exam.tip: Any valid property of graphite scores.

exam.q: Explain what happens to impurities less reactive than copper during industrial copper refining.
model: They do not form ions at the anode
and fall to the bottom as anode sludge.

exam.q: Suggest why an object must be cleaned with acid before electroplating.

exam.tip: Think about surface preparation in practical chemistry.

worked.q: A student carries out an experiment to electroplate a brass ring with copper. The initial mass of the copper anode is 5.42 g and its final mass after 30 minutes is 4.88 g. Calculate the mass loss of the anode.
steps: Calculate mass loss = Initial mass - Final mass

worked.q: Write the overall ionic equation for the transfer of copper from an impure anode to a pure cathode during copper refining.
steps: Combine equations by cancelling spectator species and electrons
